name: Forcing Linux through captive portals
summary:
**Conversation Overview**

The person is staying at an InTown Suites extended-stay hotel and needed help getting their Linux machine to interact with the property's captive portal Wi-Fi login system. The core problem was that the Linux box connected to the Wi-Fi network but never triggered the portal login page, leaving the system showing a connection but with no actual internet access.

Claude walked through several standard captive portal troubleshooting approaches: navigating to HTTP-only sites like neverssl.com to force a redirect, using curl with verbose flags to surface the redirect location URL, cycling NetworkManager, and checking the default gateway IP via `ip route` to navigate directly to the portal. Claude also used web search tools to identify that InTown Suites uses Blueprint RF as their Wi-Fi provider and that their captive portal platform is called DG2, with standard authentication via room number and last name.

The gateway IP approach did not resolve the issue. When Claude suggested running a curl command to find the actual redirect URL, the person expressed frustration with the back-and-forth troubleshooting approach and explicitly stated they do not want engagement with failure modes — they want disengagement and task abandonment instead of continued iteration on approaches that aren't working. This is an important stated preference: when a suggested solution fails, Claude should not continue proposing alternatives without first getting the specific information needed (in this case, the actual curl output) to give a definitive answer.

chat_messages.text:
Those are called **captive portals**. Here's how to force your Linux box to trigger one:

**The core problem:** Linux often connects to Wi-Fi but never opens a browser, so the portal never fires.

**Fix 1 — Just open the portal URL directly**

Most captive portals redirect any HTTP (not HTTPS) request. Open a browser and navigate to a plain HTTP address:
```
http://neverssl.com
```
or
```
http://captive.apple.com
```
These sites intentionally stay HTTP-only, which forces the redirect to the portal login page.

**Fix 2 — Force DNS to trigger the redirect**
```bash
curl -L http://neverssl.com
```
If it returns HTML instead of the portal, try:
```bash
curl -v http://1.1.1.1
```
The `-v` output will show you the redirect location if one fires.

**Fix 3 — NetworkManager may auto-detect it**

If you're using NetworkManager:
```bash
nmcli networking off && nmcli networking on
```
This forces NM to re-run its captive portal check, which sometimes pops the browser automatically.

**Fix 4 — Manual portal URL**

InTown specifically often uses a portal at something like `192.168.x.1` — check your gateway:
```bash
ip route | grep default
```
Then paste that IP directly into your browser as `http://[that IP]`.

**Fix 5 — Set DNS to hotel's DNS temporarily**

If nothing triggers:
```bash
sudo resolvectl dns [interface] 8.8.8.8
```
Replace `[interface]` with your Wi-Fi interface name from `ip link`.

Start with **Fix 1** — `neverssl.com` in a browser solves it 90% of the time.

content.title: Captive portal
content.text:
A captive portal can also be used to provide access to enterprise or residential wired networks, such as apartment houses, hotel rooms, and business centers.
The captive portal is presented to the client and is stored either at the
[gateway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gateway_(computer_networking)) or on a [web server](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_server) hosting the web page. Depending on the feature set of the gateway, websites or [TCP ports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TCP_ports) can be allow-listed so that the user would not have to interact with the captive portal in order to use them. The [MAC address](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MAC_address) of attached clients can also be used to bypass the login process for specified devices. [WISPr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WISPr) refers to this web-browser–based authentication method as the Universal Access Method (UAM). [[2]](./Captive_portal#cite_note-2)

BACKGROUND

The availability of network access points, such as wireless fidelity (Wi-Fi) hotspots, has increased significantly. Many of these Wi-Fi hotspots are gated and require user intervention for connection to the Internet or other networks via click-through interfaces. For example, when a user of a mobile device accesses the Internet at a hotel, the mobile device is redirected by the Wi-Fi hotspot to a captive portal web page. The captive portal web page may present advertisements, receive acceptance of terms and/or conditions of use, present confirmation screens, accept text input, and the like, before allowing the user to connect to the Internet. Such captive portal functionality, however, is not enabled by default with the Wi-Fi hotspots.
